pooled.text: 2 School Mental Health Quality Guide: School Mental Health Screening is part of a collection of resources developed by the National Center for School Mental Health (NCSMH) at the University of Maryland School of Medicine for The SHAPE System. The Quality Guides provide guidance to help school mental health systems advance the quality of their services and supports. This guide contains background information on school mental health screening, best practices, possible action steps, examples from the field, and resources. Recommended APA reference National Center for School Mental Health (NCSMH, 2020). School Mental Health Quality Guide: Screening. NCSMH, University of Maryland School of Medicine. The National Center for School Mental Health at the University of Maryland School of Medicine is funded by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Maternal and Child Health Bureau to advance school mental health programs and policies to promote success for America’s youth.

Conducted on a large primary care sample, the first validation study of GAD-7 found good reliability, as well as criterion, construct, factorial, and procedural validity. Subse- quently, the psychometric properties of GAD-7 have been evaluated in different sample of patients, including other primary care samples [23, 24], psychiatric patients [25–27], people with addiction [28], pregnant woman [29, 30], and outpatients [29–31]. GAD-7 has also shown strong psychometric properties in different populations, such as general adults [32], elderly [33, 34] as well as people from different culture and countries [35–39]. In academic set- ting, validation was performed among Korean university students [40], Portuguese college stu- dents [41] and Saudi university male students [42]. In the context of Bangladesh, GAD-7 has been widely used in various studies as a screening tool for anxiety symptoms among adults and university students [11–13]. Moreover, Faisal et al. (2021) explored the psychometric properties of the Bengali version of the GAD-7; however, the main focus of the paper was to assess the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on anxiety, depressive symptoms and mental health status of university students [14]. Thus, a detailed assessment of factorial validity of GAD-7 focusing on Bangladeshi students has not been carried out yet. Regardless of adequate internal consistency and moderate to strong correlation with other comorbid disorders (depression, worry, etc.), findings regarding the factor structure of GAD-7 have not been consistent [43, 44]. Indicate the number of students: • enrolled in school. • formally screened in the absence of known risk factors. • identified as being at-risk or already experiencing a mental health problem. • referred to a mental health services following identification. Document how many students were screened for each specific screening area: depression, suicidality, substance use, trauma, and other mental health concerns (e.g., ADHD, conduct, life satisfaction, academic engagement). Tips Start small: Many schools and districts have found that piloting screening procedures with small groups of students is helpful to best understand and adapt screening procedures. Starting small and scaling up to the entire student population in a gradual way allows school and district teams to make course corrections and build on successes. pooled.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015).
